claims.evidence: Supported by the scatterplot shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Under the LG+PMSF(ES60)+F+R6 model, the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 at its base) and Holosporales form a fully supported clade.
claims.source: As a first step to discriminate between these two alternatives, we used maximum likelihood to estimate a tree on a dataset that comprised 200 single-copy and rarely laterally transferred marker genes for the Alphaproteobacteria (as determined by Phyla-AMPHORA; see Materials and methods for more details; Wang and Wu, 2013) under the site-heterogenous model LG+PMSF(ES60)+F+R6. The resulting tree united the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 at its base) and Holosporales in a fully supported clade (Figure 2A; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for labeled trees).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales is suggestive of a phylogenetic artefact.
claims.source: The clustering of these three groups is suggestive of a phylogenetic artefact (e.g. long-branch attraction or LBA); indeed, such a pattern resembles the one seen in the tree of proteome amino acid compositions (see Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity to compositional clustering and known phylogenetic artifacts.

claims.claim: When 50% of the most compositionally biased sites are removed, the clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales is disrupted.
claims.source: When removing the 50% most compositionally biased (heterogeneous) sites according to ɀ (a novel metric that measures amino acid compositional disparity at a site; see Materials and methods), the clustering between the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales is disrupted (Figure 2B; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: After removing compositionally biased sites, the Pelagibacterales becomes sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
claims.source: The new more derived placements for the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales are well supported (further described below), and support tends to increase as compositionally biased sites are removed (Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary data.

claims.claim: After removing compositionally biased sites, the Holosporales becomes sister to the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: When compositional heterogeneity is further decreased by removing 50% of the most compositionally biased sites, the Holosporales becomes sister to the Rhodospirillales (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2A; and see also Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales.
claims.source: On the other hand, removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of these three long-branched groups (Supplementary file 2B), suggesting that high evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis results in Supplementary file 2B.

claims.claim: High evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
claims.source: On the other hand, removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of these three long-branched groups (Supplementary file 2B), suggesting that high evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that removing fast-evolving sites does not change the topology.

claims.claim: The Holosporales has traditionally been considered part of the Rickettsiales sensu lato because it appears as sister to the Rickettsiales in many trees.
claims.source: The Holosporales has traditionally been considered part of the Rickettsiales sensu lato because it appears as sister to the Rickettsiales in many trees (e.g. Hess et al., 2016; Montagna et al., 2013; Santos and Massard, 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The Holosporales is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes.
claims.source: It is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes, and such a lifestyle is shared with all other members of the Rickettsiales (with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean; see Castelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the lifestyle of Holosporales members, with a citation noting an exception.

claims.claim: All members of the Rickettsiales share an endosymbiotic lifestyle, with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean.
claims.source: It is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes, and such a lifestyle is shared with all other members of the Rickettsiales (with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean; see Castelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Castelli et al., 2018.

claims.claim: When compositional heterogeneity is decreased and the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, and alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 are removed, the Holosporales moves to a derived position well within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: Similarly, when the long-branched and compositionally biased Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, and alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 (plus the extremely long-branched genera Holospora and 'Candidatus Hepatobacter') are removed, after compositional heterogeneity had been decreased through site removal, the Holosporales move to a much more derived position well within the Rhodospirillales (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The Holosporales branches as sister to a subgroup of rhodospirillaleans that includes Micavibrio aeruginosavorus and Rhodocista centenaria (the Azospirillaceae).
claims.source: Specifically, the Holosporales now consistently branches as sister to a subgroup of rhodospirillaleans that includes, among others, the epibiotic predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus and the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodocista centenaria (the Azospirillaceae, see below) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The placement of the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae has nearly full support under both maximum likelihood (>95% UFBoot) and Bayesian inference (>0.95 posterior probability).
claims.source: This new placement of the Holosporales has nearly full support under both maximum likelihood (>95% UFBoot; see Figure 3) and Bayesian inference (>0.95 posterior probability; see Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical support values from phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: Three different analyses independently converge to support a derived origin of the Holosporales within the Rhodospirillales: removal of compositionally biased sites, data recoding into four-character states, and data recoding into six-character states.
claims.source: Thus, three different analyses independently converge to the same pattern and support a derived origin of the Holosporales within the Rhodospirillales: (1) removal of compositionally biased sites (Figure 3A), (2) data recoding into four-character states using the dataset-specific scheme S4 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 7), and (3) data recoding into six-character states using the dataset-specific scheme S6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8); each of these strategies had to be combined with the removal of the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59, and Rickettsiales to recover this phylogenetic position for the Holosporales.
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple independent phylogenetic analyses shown in figures.

claims.claim: Bayesian inference using the CAT-Poisson+Γ4 model on a dataset with 50% of compositionally biased sites removed recovered the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae.
claims.source: A fourth independent analysis further supports a derived placement of the Holosporales nested within the Rhodospirillales. Bayesian inference using the CAT-Poisson+Γ4 model, on a dataset whose compositional heterogeneity had been decreased by removing 50% of the most compositionally biased sites but for which no taxon had been removed, also recovered the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The Rhodospirillales comprises five well-supported families.
claims.source: Such broad sampling reveals trees with five clear subgroups within the Rhodospirillales that are well-supported in most of our analyses (e.g. Figures 2B and 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claims.claim: The Acetobacteraceae comprises acetic acid, acidophilic, and photosynthetic bacteria.
claims.source: First is the Acetobacteraceae which comprises acetic acid (e.g. Acetobacter oboediens), acidophilic (e.g. Acidisphaera rubrifaciens), and photosynthetic (bacteriochlorophyll-containing; for example, Rubritepida flocculans) bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the diversity within the Acetobacteraceae family.

claims.claim: The Acetobacteraceae is strongly supported and relatively divergent from all other families within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: The Acetobacteraceae is strongly supported and relatively divergent from all other families within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about phylogenetic support and divergence.

claims.claim: The Rhodospirillaceae includes the type species Rhodospirillum rubrum and magnetotactic bacterial genera Magnetospirillum, Magnetovibrio and Magnetospira.
claims.source: Sister to the Acetobacteraceae is another subgroup that comprises many photosynthetic bacteria, including the type species for the Rhodospirillales, Rhodospirillum rubrum, as well as the magnetotactic bacterial genera Magnetospirillum, Magnetovibrio and Magnetospira (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Rhodospirillaceae family.

claims.claim: The Holosporales is sister to the Azospirillaceae within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: As described above, when artefacts are accounted for, the Holosporales most likely branches within the Rhodospirillales and therefore we suggest the Holosporales sensu Szokoli et al. (2016) be lowered in rank to the family Holosporaceae (containing for example, Caedibacter sp. 37–49 and 'Candidatus Paracaedibacter symbiosus'), which is sister to the Azospirillaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus.
claims.source: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic (neither periplasmic nor intracellular) predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus, among others.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Azospirillaceae family.

claims.claim: Micavibrio aeruginosavorus is an epibiotic predator that is neither periplasmic nor intracellular.
claims.source: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic (neither periplasmic nor intracellular) predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus, among others.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the lifestyle of Micavibrio aeruginosavorus.

claims.claim: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae.
claims.source: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3), a well-supported group that comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The Rhodovibriaceae comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
claims.source: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3), a well-supported group that comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Rhodovibriaceae family.

claims.claim: The Geminicoccaceae is a recently proposed family within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: The Geminicocacceae is a recently proposed family within the Rhodospirillales (Proença et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Proença et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The Geminicoccaceae is currently represented by two genera, Geminicoccus and Arboriscoccus.
claims.source: It is currently represented by only two genera, Geminicoccus and Arboriscoccus (Foesel et al., 2007; Proença et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Foesel et al., 2007 and Proença et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Tistrella mobilis is often sister to Geminicoccus roseus with full statistical support.
claims.source: In most of our trees, however, Tistrella mobilis is often sister to Geminicoccus roseus with full statistical support (e.g., Figures 2B and 3A, but see Figure 3—figure supplement 6 for an exception) and we therefore consider it to be part of the Geminococcaceae.
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The Geminicoccaceae tends to have two alternative stable positions in the analyses: either as sister to all other families of the Rhodospirillales, or as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Geminicoccaceae tends to have two alternative stable positions in our analyses, either as sister to all other families of the Rhodospirillales (e.g. Figures 2A and 3A), or as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae (i.e. representing the most basal lineage of free-living alphaproteobacteria; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 6, or Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Analyses designed to alleviate compositional heterogeneity favor the placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae.
claims.source: Our analyses designed to alleviate compositional heterogeneity, specifically site removal and recoding (without taxon removal), favor the latter position for the Geminicoccaceae (Figures 2B and 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3B.

claims.claim: As compositionally biased sites are progressively removed, support for the affiliation of the Geminicoccaceae with the Rhodospirillales decreases.
claims.source: Moreover, as compositionally biased sites are progressively removed, support for the affiliation of the Geminicoccaceae with the Rhodospirillales decreases, and after 50% of the sites have been removed, the Geminicoccaceae emerges as sister to all other free-living alphaproteobacteria with strong support (>95% UFBoot; Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with progressive site removal shown in Supplementary file 2A.

claims.claim: The LG4X model places the Geminicoccaceae in a derived position as sister to the Acetobacteraceae.
claims.source: In further agreement with this trend, the much simpler model LG4X places the Geminicocacceae in a derived position as sister to the Acetobacteraceae (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), but as model complexity increases, and compositional heterogeneity is reduced, the Geminicoccaceae moves closer to the base of the Alphaproteobacteria (Figures 2A and 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The Geminicoccaceae may be a novel and independent order-level lineage in the Alphaproteobacteria.
claims.source: Such a placement suggests that the Geminicoccaceae may be a novel and independent order-level lineage in the Alphaproteobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic placement.

claims.claim: The removal of compositionally biased sites (from 30% on) supports a derived placement of the Pelagibacterales as sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
claims.source: The removal of compositionally biased sites (from 30% on; 16,320 out of 54,400 sites; see Supplementary file 2A, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), data recoding into four-character states (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), and a set of the most compositionally homogeneous genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), all support a derived placement of the Pelagibacterales as sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The Caulobacterales is sister to the Rhizobiales, and the Rhodobacterales is sister to both.
claims.source: The Caulobacterales is sister to the Rhizobiales, and the Rhodobacterales sister to both (e.g. Figures 2B and 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claims.claim: The interrelationships among Caulobacterales, Rhizobiales, and Rhodobacterales become very robustly supported as compositional heterogeneity is increasingly alleviated.
claims.source: This is consistent throughout most of our results and such interrelationships become very robustly supported as compositional heterogeneity is increasingly alleviated (Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with progressive site removal shown in Supplementary file 2A.

claims.claim: The placement of the Rickettsiales as sister to the Caulobacteridae remains stable across different analyses.
claims.source: The placement of the Rickettsiales as sister to the Caulobacteridae (i.e. all other alphaproteobacteria) remains stable across different analyses (see Supplementary file 2A, and also Figure 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2); this is also true when the other long-branched taxa, the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales, and even the Beta- Gammaproteobacteria outgroup, are removed (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures and supplementary files.

claims.claim: The interrelationships inside the Rickettsiales order remain uncertain.
claims.source: Yet, the interrelationships inside the Rickettsiales order remain uncertain; the 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae' becomes sister to the Anaplasmataceae when fast-evolving sites are removed (Supplementary file 2B), but to the Rickettsiaceae when compositionally biased sites are removed (Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with different site removal strategies shown in supplementary files.

claims.claim: The placement of alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is uncertain.
claims.source: The placement of alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is uncertain (e.g. see Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5; in contrast to Grote et al., 2012); taxon-removal analyses suggest that alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is sister to the Caulobacteridae (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), but the inclusion of any other long-branched group immediately destabilizes this position (e.g. see Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is not closely related to the Pelagibacterales.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous reports that suggest that alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is not closely related to the Pelagibacterales (Viklund et al., 2013; Martijn et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Viklund et al., 2013 and Martijn et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The Rickettsiales sensu lato (i.e. the Rickettsiales and Holosporales) is polyphyletic.
claims.source: A combination of these strategies reveals that the Rickettsiales sensu lato (i.e. the Rickettsiales and Holosporales) is polyphyletic.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic analyses presented.

claims.claim: The Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: Our analyses suggest that the Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales, and that therefore this taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family (see Figures 2B and 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claims.claim: The Holosporales taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family.
claims.source: Our analyses suggest that the Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales, and that therefore this taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family (see Figures 2B and 3).
claims.evidence: This is a taxonomic proposal based on phylogenetic results.

claims.claim: The Rhodospirillales might be a paraphyletic order.
claims.source: The same methods suggest that the Rhodospirillales might indeed be a paraphyletic order and that the Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae (e.g. Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae.
claims.source: The same methods suggest that the Rhodospirillales might indeed be a paraphyletic order and that the Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae (e.g. Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The diversity of the Rhodospirillales can be grouped into at least five well-supported major families.
claims.source: These two results, combined with our broader sampling, reorganize the internal phylogenetic structure of the Rhodospirillales and show that its diversity can be grouped into at least five well-supported major families (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The apparent diversity of the Holosporales has quickly increased in recent years as more intracellular bacteria living within protists have been described.
claims.source: The apparent diversity of this group has quickly increased in recent years as more and more intracellular bacteria living within protists have been described (e.g. Hess et al., 2016; Szokoli et al., 2016; Eschbach et al., 2009; Boscaro et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies describing new members.

claims.claim: Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015) provided apparent strong support for the monophyly of the Rickettsiales and the Holosporales based on multi-gene trees.
claims.source: Apparent strong support for the monophyly of the Rickettsiales and the Holosporales recently came from some multi-gene trees by Wang and Wu (2014), and Wang and Wu (2015) who expanded sampling for the Holosporales.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015).

claims.claim: An alternative placement for the Holosporales as sister to the Caulobacteridae has been reported by multiple studies.
claims.source: However, an alternative placement for the Holosporales as sister to the Caulobacteridae has been reported by Ferla et al. (2013) based on rRNA genes, by Georgiades et al. (2011) based on 65 genes, by Schulz et al., (2015) based on 139 genes, as well as by Wang and Wu (2015) based on 26, 29, or 200 genes (see the supplementary information in Wang and Wu, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Szokoli et al. (2016) formally established the order Holosporales.
claims.source: This placement was acknowledged by Szokoli et al. (2016), who formally established the order Holosporales.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Szokoli et al. (2016).

claims.claim: Martijn et al. (2018) recovered a number of placements for the Holosporales within the Alphaproteobacteria, but these different placements were poorly supported.
claims.source: Most recently, Martijn et al. (2018), who used strategies to reduce compositional heterogeneity, and similarly to Wang and Wu (2015), recovered a number of placements for the Holosporales within the Alphaproteobacteria; however, these different placements for the Holosporales were poorly supported.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Martijn et al. (2018).

claims.claim: This study provides strong evidence for the hypothesis that the Holosporales is not related to the Rickettsiales.
claims.source: Here, we provide strong evidence for the hypothesis that the Holosporales is not related to the Rickettsiales, as suggested earlier (Georgiades et al., 2011; Ferla et al., 2013; Szokoli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic analyses presented, with citations to earlier studies that suggested this hypothesis.

claims.claim: The Holosporales is artefactually attracted to the Rickettsiales.
claims.source: We show that the Holosporales is artefactually attracted to the Rickettsiales (e.g. Figure 2A), but as compositional bias is increasingly alleviated (through site removal and recoding), they move further away from them (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: The Holosporales is placed within the Rhodopirillales as sister to the family Azospirillaceae.
claims.source: The Holosporales is placed within the Rhodopirillales as sister to the family Azospirillaceae (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The similar lifestyles of the Holosporales and Rickettsiales are likely the outcome of convergent evolution.
claims.source: The similar lifestyles of the Holosporales and Rickettsiales, as well as other features like the presence of an ATP/ADP translocase (Wang and Wu, 2014), are therefore likely the outcome of convergent evolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic separation of the two groups.

claims.claim: Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015) proposed that mitochondria are phylogenetically embedded within the Rickettsiales sensu lato.
claims.source: Wang and Wu (2014), and Wang and Wu (2015) proposed that mitochondria are phylogenetically embedded within the Rickettsiales sensu lato.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015).

claims.claim: In the trees of Wang and Wu (2014, 2015), mitochondria were sister to a clade formed by the Rickettsiaceae, Anaplasmataceae and 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae', and the Holosporales was itself sister to all of them.
claims.source: In their trees, mitochondria were sister to a clade formed by the Rickettsiaceae, Anaplasmataceae and 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae', and the Holosporales was itself sister to all of them.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic placement in the trees of Wang and Wu (2014, 2015).

claims.claim: Wang and Wu (2014) suggested that the ancestor of mitochondria was an intracellular parasite based on the phylogenetic placement of mitochondria.
claims.source: This phylogenetic placement for mitochondria suggested that the ancestor of mitochondria was an intracellular parasite (Wang and Wu, 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Wu (2014).

claims.claim: If the Holosporales is a derived group of rhodospirillaleans, then the argument that mitochondria necessarily evolved from parasitic alphaproteobacteria no longer holds.
claims.source: But if the Holosporales is a derived group of rhodospirillaleans as we show here (see Figure 3), then the argument that mitochondria necessarily evolved from parasitic alphaproteobacteria no longer holds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic results presented.

claims.claim: The sisterhood of mitochondria and the Rickettsiales sensu stricto does not imply that the two groups shared a parasitic common ancestor.
claims.source: While the sisterhood of mitochondria and the Rickettsiales sensu stricto is still a possibility, such a relationship does not imply that the two groups shared a parasitic common ancestor (i.e. a parasitic ancestry for mitochondria).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic results.

claims.claim: Martijn et al. (2018) suggest that mitochondria are sister to all known alphaproteobacteria, suggesting their non-parasitic ancestry.
claims.source: The most recent analyses of Martijn et al. (2018) suggest that mitochondria are sister to all known alphaproteobacteria, also suggesting their non-parasitic ancestry.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Martijn et al. (2018).

claims.claim: Mitochondria most likely evolved from ancestral free-living alphaproteobacteria.
claims.source: Our study, and that of Martijn et al., thus complement each other and support the view that mitochondria most likely evolved from ancestral free-living alphaproteobacteria (contra Sassera et al., 2011; Wang and Wu, 2014; Wang and Wu, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic results of this study and Martijn et al. (2018), with citations to contrasting views.

claims.claim: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae.
claims.source: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae and has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic position and historical taxonomy of the Rhodospirillales.

claims.claim: The Rhodospirillales has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
claims.source: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae and has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about historical taxonomy.

claims.claim: A new family, the Geminicoccaceae, was recently established for the Rhodospirillales.
claims.source: Recently, a new family, the Geminicoccaceae, was established for the Rhodospirillales (Proença et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Proença et al. (2018).

claims.claim: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available.
claims.source: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available; if it were to be confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research and a conditional taxonomic proposal.

claims.claim: If the placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae is confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.
claims.source: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available; if it were to be confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.

results.result: Three novel endosymbiotic alphaproteobacterial genomes were sequenced and characterized: 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata' (Holosporales), a Stachyamoeba-associated rickettsialean (Rickettsiales), and a Peranema-associated rickettsialean (Rickettsiales). All three genomes are small with reduced gene numbers and high A+T% content, consistent with an endosymbiotic lifestyle.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C27 provide genome characteristics (size, composition, taxonomic placement) for three novel endosymbionts. The data in Table 1 and sequence comparisons support these characterizations. The inference of endosymbiotic lifestyle from genome features (C25) is reasonable given established patterns in endosymbionts.

results.result: The Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59), and Holosporales have divergent proteome amino acid compositions compared to other alphaproteobacteria, characterized by the lowest GARP:FIMNKY ratios. This compositional bias correlates strongly with A+T%-rich genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 describe compositional patterns supported by clustering analysis (Figure 1A) and scatterplot data (Figure 1B). The relationship between codon usage (C30-C31) and genome composition (C32-C33) is well-established. The data clearly demonstrate the compositional distinctiveness of these three groups.

results.result: Under standard phylogenetic models, the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, and Holosporales form a fully supported clade, but this clustering is disrupted when compositionally biased sites are removed. Removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering, indicating that compositional heterogeneity, not evolutionary rate, is the major confounding factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 describe phylogenetic patterns under different analytical conditions. The results are supported by multiple phylogenetic analyses (Figures 2A, 2B, supplementary files). The differential effect of removing compositionally biased versus fast-evolving sites (C36, C39) provides strong evidence that compositional bias is the primary artifact. The inference about confounding factors (C40) is well-justified.

results.result: The Holosporales, traditionally considered sister to the Rickettsiales, is actually derived within the Rhodospirillales as sister to the Azospirillaceae. This placement is recovered by multiple independent analyses (site removal, four-state recoding, six-state recoding, Bayesian inference) with strong statistical support (>95% UFBoot, >0.95 posterior probability).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 present the major phylogenetic finding of the study. The result is supported by convergent evidence from four independent analytical strategies (C47-C48), all showing consistent placement with high statistical support (C46). The analyses appropriately address compositional bias and long-branch attraction. The requirement to remove long-branched taxa (C44) is a limitation but is justified given the strong compositional biases.

results.result: The Rhodospirillales comprises five well-supported families: Acetobacteraceae, Rhodospirillaceae (restricted), Holosporaceae (formerly Holosporales), Azospirillaceae (new), and Rhodovibriaceae (new). The Holosporaceae is sister to the Azospirillaceae, and together they are sister to the Rhodovibriaceae.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 describe the internal structure of the Rhodospirillales. The five-family structure is supported by phylogenetic analyses (Figures 2B, 3) with strong support values. The descriptions of family composition (C50, C52, C54, C57) are factual. The sister-group relationships (C53, C56) are supported by the phylogenetic data.

results.result: The Geminicoccaceae (including Tistrella mobilis) has two alternative phylogenetic positions: either sister to all other Rhodospirillales families, or sister to all other Caulobacteridae orders. Analyses designed to reduce compositional heterogeneity favor the latter placement, suggesting the Geminicoccaceae may represent a novel order-level lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 describe an unstable phylogenetic placement for the Geminicoccaceae. While the two alternative positions are documented (C61) and compositional bias reduction favors one placement (C62-C63), the authors acknowledge uncertainty and conservatively retain the family within Rhodospirillales. The speculation about order-level status (C65) is appropriately tentative. More data are needed to resolve this placement definitively.

results.result: The Pelagibacterales has a derived placement as sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales, and Rhizobiales. The Caulobacterales is sister to the Rhizobiales, and the Rhodobacterales is sister to both. These relationships become robustly supported as compositional heterogeneity is alleviated.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 describe the placement of the Pelagibacterales and relationships among other orders. Multiple analytical strategies converge on this topology (C66), and support increases with compositional bias reduction (C68). The phylogenetic data (Figures 2B, 3, Supplementary file 2A) support these relationships.

results.result: The Rickettsiales is stably placed as sister to the Caulobacteridae across different analyses, but internal relationships within the Rickettsiales remain uncertain, varying depending on whether compositionally biased or fast-evolving sites are removed.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 describe the phylogenetic position of the Rickettsiales. The stable placement as sister to Caulobacteridae is supported by multiple analyses (C69, supplementary files). The uncertainty about internal relationships (C70) is appropriately acknowledged and documented with different analytical outcomes.

results.result: The phylogenetic placement of alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is uncertain, with taxon-removal analyses suggesting it is sister to the Caulobacteridae, but this position is destabilized by inclusion of other long-branched groups. It is not closely related to the Pelagibacterales.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 describe the uncertain placement of HIMB59. The instability is documented across multiple analyses (C71, various figures), and the lack of relationship to Pelagibacterales (C72) is consistent with previous studies (citations provided). The uncertainty is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: The Rickettsiales sensu lato (Rickettsiales + Holosporales) is polyphyletic. The Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales as sister to the Azospirillaceae and should be lowered in rank to the family Holosporaceae. The similar endosymbiotic lifestyles of Holosporales and Rickettsiales are likely the result of convergent evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C84-C87 present the main conclusion about the polyphyly of Rickettsiales sensu lato. This is strongly supported by the phylogenetic analyses showing separation of the two groups (C85, Figure 2A vs 2B) and the derived placement of Holosporales (C74, C86, Figure 3). The inference of convergent evolution (C87) is reasonable given the phylogenetic separation. The taxonomic proposal (C75) follows logically from the phylogenetic results.

results.result: The derived placement of the Holosporales within the Rhodospirillales undermines previous arguments that mitochondria necessarily evolved from parasitic alphaproteobacteria. Combined with recent analyses suggesting mitochondria are sister to all alphaproteobacteria, the evidence supports a free-living ancestry for mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 discuss implications for mitochondrial origins. The logic is sound: if Holosporales is not sister to Rickettsiales (as shown in this study), then previous arguments for parasitic mitochondrial ancestry based on that relationship (C88-C90) no longer hold (C91-C92). The inference about free-living ancestry (C94) is appropriately cautious and supported by convergent evidence from this study and Martijn et al. (2018).

results.result: The Rhodospirillaceae sensu lato is subdivided into three subgroups: Rhodospirillaceae sensu stricto (sister to Acetobacteraceae), Azospirillaceae (sister to Holosporaceae), and Rhodovibriaceae.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 describe the taxonomic reorganization of the Rhodospirillaceae. This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses (Figure 3) showing clear separation of these groups with strong support. The taxonomic proposals follow logically from the phylogenetic results.

results.result: An updated higher-level taxonomy of the Alphaproteobacteria is proposed, comprising two subclasses (Rickettsidae and Caulobacteridae), with the Caulobacteridae containing seven orders. The Magnetococcales is excluded from Alphaproteobacteria and placed in the Magnetococcia class. The Rhodospirillales comprises six families, three of which are newly described.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C116 present the taxonomic synthesis. The proposals are based on the phylogenetic results presented throughout the study (Table 2). The exclusion of Magnetococcales (C107-C108) is supported by citation to previous work. The taxonomic structure follows logically from the phylogenetic framework established in the study.

results.result: The study employed a dataset of 200 single-copy, predominantly vertically inherited genes and developed multiple methodological innovations to address compositional bias, including a novel metric (ɀ) for measuring compositional disparity, dataset-specific profile mixture models, and recoding schemes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C128 describe the methodological approach. The dataset characteristics (C123-C124) are documented and cited. The novel metric ɀ (C125) is described in the methods. The use of multiple strategies to reduce compositional bias (C126-C128) is documented throughout the results and methods sections. These methodological innovations are central to the study's ability to address phylogenetic artifacts.

results.result: The study demonstrates that the Rickettsiales and Holosporales, both groups of intracellular parasites, are not sisters to each other, with the Holosporales having a derived position within the Rhodospirillales. This provides an updated phylogenetic framework for placing mitochondria and novel environmental diversity within the Alphaproteobacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 summarize the main findings and their significance. The phylogenetic results (C129-C130) are strongly supported by the analyses presented. The statement about utility for future research (C133) is reasonable given the comprehensive phylogenetic framework established, though it is somewhat speculative about future applications.

results.result: Background claims establish that the Alphaproteobacteria is a diverse group encompassing the mitochondrial lineage and eight major orders, with diverse genome compositions and evolutionary rates that can lead to phylogenetic artifacts such as long-branch attraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 provide background context supported by citations to previous literature. These are well-established facts about Alphaproteobacteria diversity, taxonomy, and known phylogenetic challenges. The citations support the claims about diversity (C1-C4), taxonomic structure (C5-C7), compositional variation (C8-C11), and phylogenetic artifacts (C12).

results.result: Previous studies have provided conflicting evidence about the phylogenetic position of the Holosporales, with some supporting monophyly with Rickettsiales and others suggesting alternative placements, though with poor support.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 review previous literature on Holosporales phylogeny. The claims are supported by appropriate citations documenting the conflicting results in the literature. This provides important context for the current study's contribution to resolving this uncertainty.

results.result: The Rhodospirillales has historically been subdivided into two families (Rhodospirillaceae and Acetobacteraceae), with a third (Geminicoccaceae) recently established. The Acetobacteraceae is well-defined, but there has been uncertainty about the Rhodospirillaceae. The placement of Geminicoccaceae requires further testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C101 provide background on Rhodospirillales taxonomy and acknowledge uncertainties. The historical taxonomy (C95-C96) and recent additions (C97) are supported by citations. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C98-C99, C101) and the statement about Acetobacteraceae being well-defined (C100) are appropriate contextual statements.

results.result: The proposed classification could be partly harmonized with that of Parks et al. (2018) by elevating families to order level, but there are conflicts between the trees and proposed taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 discuss the relationship between this study's taxonomy and that of Parks et al. (2018). The acknowledgment of both potential harmonization and conflicts is appropriate and supported by the citation. This provides useful context about how the current work relates to other recent taxonomic proposals.

results.result: A robust phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria is necessary for placing mitochondria, as including mitochondria exacerbates compositional biases. The phylogenetic framework developed here will serve as a reference for future studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 discuss the importance and utility of the study. The statement about the need for a robust framework (C119) is logical. The observation about mitochondria exacerbating biases (C120) is supported by citation to Wang and Wu (2015). The claim about future utility (C121) is somewhat speculative but reasonable given the comprehensive framework established.

results.result: Cultures of Viridiraptor invadens strain Virl02 were grown on the filamentous green alga Zygnema pseudogedeanum strain CCAC 0199 as described in Hess and Melkonian (2013).
results.evaluation: Claim C122 describes the culture method with appropriate citation. This is a straightforward methodological detail that is adequately documented.

results.result: The Rhodospirillales might be a paraphyletic order, with the Geminicoccaceae potentially representing a separate lineage sister to the Caulobacteridae.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 present speculative conclusions about the paraphyly of Rhodospirillales. While some analyses support this (Figure 2B), the authors acknowledge uncertainty and conservatively retain the current classification. The speculation is appropriately cautious but the evidence is not conclusive enough to definitively support this result.

results.result: The diversity of the Rhodospirillales can be grouped into at least five well-supported major families.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 summarizes the reorganization of Rhodospirillales. This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses (Figure 3) showing five distinct, well-supported clades. The use of "at least" is appropriately cautious given potential undiscovered diversity.
